method_1: paragraph URL session differs from bill key session: 10,926 of 65,813 (16.6%)
method_2: API session field differs from bill key session: 10,926 (16.6%); URL and API disagree with each other on 0 of 65,809
conclusion: WRONG if both methods show mismatches while URL and API agree with each other: the hand-written session table is the error, not the API.

method_1: paragraphs under procedural headings (Business of the House, Third Readings, etc.) that were assigned to a bill: 5,204
method_2: (bill, date, heading) blocks assigned by bill-number-in-text with no procedural anchor for that bill: 737 of 1,185 (62.2%)
conclusion: Every one of these is a paragraph that mentions a bill without debating it.

method_1: health-bill index dates with no fetched text for that bill: 1,891 of 2,952 (64.1%)
method_2: index dates where no procedural anchor names that bill in any fetched paragraph that day: 2,480 (84.0%)
conclusion: The index dates record mentions, and the scraper only fetched those dates, so real debate days outside the index were never collected.

method_1: sentences dated on days that do not exist in the current segments: 1,096,198 of 1,942,246 (56.4%)
method_2: sentence IDs in the OLD era format (e.g. -api-1985b32-): 1,942,246; in session format: 0
conclusion: If either number is large, predications, triples and scores were computed on the OLD corpus, so no Ontario result reported after the rescrape was derived from the rescrape.

method_1: (parliament, bill number) keys that exist in more than one session of the FSOB file: 370 (compute_factuality_scores.py joins on parliament, so these take the wrong session's outcome)
method_2: dates with two or more health bills in the index: 743 (the score script keys bill metadata by date, so one bill overwrites the other)
conclusion: Both joins must use the full key: session plus bill number.

method_1: sampled sentences detected as French: 2,042 of 215,806 (0.9%)
method_2: predications whose subject+verb+object read as French: 5,535 of 197,316
conclusion: Every one of these went through en_core_web_lg and Spotlight EN (e.g. 'ai' linked to Artificial_intelligence).

method_2: of those, bills whose assigned Hansard headings also contain no health term: 26
conclusion: These need a manual yes/no from Joanie and David before they stay in the corpus.

method_2: files that begin mid-sentence (first letter lowercase): 3,412 (40.8%)
conclusion: A file that never names its bill, or starts mid-sentence, was cut by a marker that fired in the wrong place.

method_2: same debates where the bill number appears in ANY file of that date: 735 (60.9%)

method_1: files whose filename date differs from the date printed in the Record header: 95 of 240
method_2: files from the bound edition (Pt. N) instead of the daily edition (Vol. N, No. N): 84 of 448 (daily edition headers found: 366)
conclusion: Late-night sittings put the vote on the next calendar day. The debate lives in the Record of the legislative day, and David wants the daily edition issue.

method_2: lines where bill section text (SEC. 2, SECTION 1) is glued onto speech text: 100
conclusion: Both patterns mean two columns were read across as one line.

method_2: files naming more than 3 distinct H.R. numbers: 364 of 448
conclusion: These files are whole days or whole sections, not one bill's debate, so the US denominator was never bill specific.
